results.severity_observed: P2 — real, deterministic, but conditional on provider behaviour rather than attacker-controllable (see notes)
results.notes:
REACHABILITY: fully reachable at the real edge — POST /api/provider-verification-callback is a public webhook endpoint whose only credential is the shared IDFY_WEBHOOK_SECRET. No internal-only call needed.
ARGUING IT IS CORRECT REPLAY BEHAVIOUR, from the code's own stated intent: the module header states the dedup contract as 'Deduplication on the provider's own event id with a UNIQUE index, so a redelivery (providers retry on any non-2xx) answers 200 and changes no state.' Under a well-behaved webhook provider an event id identifies one immutable event; a redelivery carries the same body, so keying on the id alone is exactly right and answering 200 is what stops the retry storm. The signature covers the body, so an attacker cannot substitute a different outcome under a captured event id — the second body must be signed with the real secret, i.e. it must genuinely come from IDfy. On that reading nothing is wrong.
ARGUING IT IS A KYC-TRUTH DEFECT, from the same file: the long comment above the UPDATE says outright that 'verified may still become failed (a later revocation) and failed may still become verified (a correction)' and that both 'are the provider's own judgement'. The event-id-only key silently vetoes precisely that intent whenever the provider reuses or redelivers an id with a new decision — my CALL 3 control proves the identical revocation IS honoured under a fresh id, so the monotonicity engine wants to apply it and only the dedup gate stops it. Worse, the code computes payload_sha256 of every body and stores it, then never compares it: the one field that could distinguish 'same event, same body' (a true replay) from 'same event, different body' (a changed decision) is collected and discarded. And the response is affirmatively wrong rather than merely stale — it returns accepted:true with an outcome the database does not hold (demonstrated above: reply 'verified' while the row reads 'failed'), which is the one thing the file's own comment on the earlier 404-poisoning bug says must not happen ('the response claimed success').
MY READING: it is a genuine truth defect, correctly rated below the other six. A stale KYC 'verified' persisting after the provider has revoked it is exactly the wrong direction to fail — but it requires IDfy to reuse an event id for a changed outcome, which a conformant provider will not do, and it is not reachable by anyone without the webhook secret.

results.repeatable: Yes. The duplicate-trigger probe ran 3 times, identical each run: 500 response, host mandate reduced from 4 rows to 1 (aadhaar, updated_by ops@pawspace.test), canTakeAssignments false -> true. The four fail-safe cases ran once each within a 6-case sweep and left the table untouched every time.
results.notes: IMPORTANT — the candidate's own hinted triggers do NOT reproduce it. Every validation in setCategoryMandate (unknown category line 92, non-array line 93, unknown verification type line 97, empty list line 99) runs BEFORE the DELETE at line 101, so all of them fail safe with the mandate fully intact. I confirmed that by execution for all four. The only input I found that gets past validation and then fails mid-write is a DUPLICATE entry in verificationTypes, which the function does not de-duplicate. The claim 'defaults are never reseeded' is also FALSE as stated: I wiped all host rows directly and then called requiredVerifications('host'), and seedDefaultMandates restored all four defaults (it skips a category only when COUNT(*)>0). Defaults are not reseeded in the duplicate case purely because the first INSERT succeeded and left one row behind. So the mechanism (DELETE commits, re-INSERT does not) is real and reachable through POST /api/provider-verification with providers.manage, but the effect is a silently TRUNCATED mandate rather than a destroyed one, and the trigger is a duplicate list entry, not a rejected type or an empty list. The 500 is also an ungoverned generic error, so the operator is told nothing about what was lost.

results.repeatable: Yes. Run 3 times; every run produced outcome "verified"/duplicate true on the second delivery with provider_verifications unchanged, and the control delivery under a fresh event id flipped the row to 'failed'. The stored payload_sha256 was byte-identical (b9526eac...) across all runs and never updated by delivery 2.
results.notes: Judged against the module's own stated intent, this is a KYC-truth defect, not correct replay behaviour. The docblock defines the guarantee as 'Deduplication on the provider's own event id with a UNIQUE index, so a REDELIVERY (providers retry on any non-2xx) answers 200 and CHANGES NO STATE' — a redelivery is by definition the same payload. Delivery 2 is not a redelivery: it is a different body carrying the opposite decision, and the code has the exact evidence needed to tell them apart. payload_sha256 is computed on every request and stored on the callback row, and it is never read back or compared anywhere in the file. The same block also states 'A terminal outcome may overwrite anything (verified -> failed is a revocation, failed -> verified a correction; both are the provider's own judgement and both were already approved)' — the monotonic UPDATE deliberately permits exactly the transition that the event-id dedup silently swallows, and the control delivery proves the write path works. So the module explicitly wants revocations applied and explicitly wants only identical redeliveries short-circuited; keying on event id alone collapses the two. Consequence: a provider whose Aadhaar/PAN is later revoked by IDfy under a reused event id keeps status='verified', keeps canTakeAssignments=true, and IDfy is told 200 ok so it stops retrying. Contrary argument, stated fairly: a webhook event id is meant to identify one immutable event, so IDfy re-sending a different outcome under the same id is arguably provider misbehaviour, and answering 200 stops a retry storm. That argument does not survive the file's own text, because it would also require the boundary to record the contradiction as evidence — the file says 'a rejected callback is evidence too, so it is never dropped' — and here nothing is recorded at all.
